speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: asked the Minister for Trade and Industry (a) what are the sectoral productivity growth rates, trends and outlook in Singapore since the onset of COVID-19; and (b) whether there are new measures or productivity needed to better measure the hybrid model of work productivity.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: By contrast, sectors which were severely disrupted by travel and domestic restrictions, such as construction, transportation and storage, accommodation and F&B services, experienced declines in productivity.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: For 2021, productivity growth is expected to remain positive for the most outward-oriented sectors, given the pick-up in global economic activity.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: Sectors that continue to be disrupted by weak travel demand and domestic restrictions such as transportation and storage and F&B services, are not likely to return to pre-COVID-19 productivity levels, as activities in these sectors are not expected to recover fully this year.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: Since 2015, the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) has compiled statistics on real value-added per actual hour worked, to complement statistics on real value-added per worker.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: Real value-added per actual hour worked is recognised internationally, including by the International Labour Organization (ILO), to be the most appropriate measure of labour productivity as actual hours worked capture the intensity of labour input more accurately.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: These include (a) flexi-time arrangements that grant employees flexible work schedules, depending on their work, of course, and personal commitments; (b) flexi-load arrangements that involve employees who are hired on a part-time or project basis; as well as (c) flexi-place arrangements that allow employees to telecommute and record hours worked in both workplace settings and at home.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: First is in relation to my earlier Parliamentary Question (PQ), can the Minister of State share about the outlook for the productivity by sector, if possible, in 2022; and beyond 2022, given growth and other variables?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The second supplementary question I have is, in relation to the second part of my PQ.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Are there plans for MTI to do any further granular data studies to examine productivity, in terms of both labour and multi-factor productivity, especially during the COVID-19 period and possibly into the endemic period?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The reason is, if we look at the actual hours worked data, which is good that it is in quarterly basis, whether there will be more measures that MTI plans to collect, going forward, similar to what other developed countries like in the US, so as to measure productivity more accurately, going forward?

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I will take the measurement of labour productivity first and then go into the outlook across sectors.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: First is on how is labour productivity typically measured and what are the differences between existing labour productivity measures?

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Labour productivity measures actually measure how effectively or efficiently labour inputs are used to produce output.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: They are computed in terms of, as I mentioned, real value-added (VA) per actual hour worked, or real VA per worker.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: There are differences between these two because of changes in the average number of hours worked per worker over time.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I think that also has been quite accentuated during COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: In Singapore's context, this measure has also become more relevant in recent years with the rising number of part-time workers in the economy and the cyclical changes in the number of hours worked by full-time workers.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: If you look at TFP or Total Factor Productivity, which is also known as multi-factor productivity, is also an alternate measure of productivity and captures how efficiently both capital and labour are used together in the production process.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: It is computed as a residual on an annual basis and is defined as a change in GDP not attributed to changes in capital and labour inputs.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, for example, an increase in TFP may be due to factors such as a rise in technology, improvements in management practices and organisational structures or maybe even the diffusion of technology across firms.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, while not a 100% accurate indication, I think this particular measure, for now, manages to capture productivity in the most accurate form.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But we will be open to looking at other ways to measure, given the changing nature of work across the world and given how COVID-19 has also looked at productivity across workplace and at home.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: With regards to the outlook for productivity, both Minister of State Low and myself have shared earlier on that the growth as well as recovery across sectors are uneven.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: There are domestically oriented sectors and there are the outwardly oriented sectors.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But our productivity performance tends to be pro-cyclical and so it has resulted in an uneven productivity across various sectors.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I wanted to also just share a little bit that what we are doing is we are not being stagnant in this regard, productivity has been an issue in advanced economies and in particular, Singapore has been managing or trying to increase productivity for decades.
